query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Localized elemental segregation at grain boundaries in the as-built additive manufacturing microstructure creates heterogeneous regions that govern non-uniform formation of protective oxide scales, thereby driving degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an FCC matrix, in which rapid solidification may lead to slight grain boundary segregation of reactive elements such as Cr and Ti.
generation.intervention: Implement a post-build annealing treatment at a moderate temperature (approximately 800–900 °C for a short duration) to homogenize the grain boundary composition without significant coarsening of the FCC structure.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures (700–1000 °C) in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Improved compositional uniformity at grain boundaries facilitates the formation of a continuous, coherent, and protective oxide scale across the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Local segregation at grain boundaries can result in areas enriched or depleted in key elements responsible for forming protective oxides (e.g., Cr). This compositional inhomogeneity can lead to a patchy oxide scale, accelerating degradation by creating weak spots. A controlled annealing treatment promotes atomic diffusion that homogenizes the distribution of these elements at the grain boundaries, thereby ensuring a more uniform oxide formation during high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples should display more uniform grain boundary composition, as evidenced by EPMA/EDS, and a correspondingly continuous and adherent oxide scale with lower weight gain over time compared to as-built samples.
generation.baseline: As-built alloy with potential for minor elemental segregation at grain boundaries resulting in non-uniform oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected under high-temperature conditions (>700 °C) in both oxidizing and reducing environments where diffusion is active but the FCC matrix is maintained.
generation.uncertainty: The degree of initial elemental segregation and the efficacy of the annealing treatment in eliminating it may vary; precise quantification is challenging.

Creep resistance is dependent, in part, on slowing the speed of dislocation motion within a crystal structure. In modern Ni-based superalloys, the γ'-Ni3(Al,Ti) phase acts as a barrier to dislocation. For this reason, this γ;' intermetallic phase, when present in high volume fractions, increases the strength of these alloys due to its ordered nature and high coherency with the γ matrix. The chemical additions of aluminum and titanium promote the creation of the γ' phase. The γ' phase size can be precisely controlled by careful precipitation strengthening heat treatments. Many superalloys are produced using a two-phase heat treatment that creates a dispersion of cuboidal γ' particles known as the primary phase, with a fine dispersion between these known as secondary γ'. In order to improve the oxidation resistance of these alloys, Al, Cr, B, and Y are added. The Al and Cr form oxide layers that passivate the surface and protect the superalloy from further oxidation while B and Y are used to improve the adhesion of this oxide scale to the substrate. paper_did: Prepared a series of FeNiCuAl‐based high‐entropy alloys: the Base Alloy (equiatomic FeNiCuAl), the Synergy Alloy (Base Alloy with 2.5 at.% each of Cr, Co, and Mn), and the Innovation Alloy (Synergy Alloy with an additional 0.5 at.% Y).

Employed two fabrication methods: conventional vacuum arc melting (for Base and Synergy Alloys) and laser cladding (for the Innovation Alloy coating on a Synergy substrate) to induce nanocrystallization.

Conducted extensive high‐temperature performance tests including isothermal oxidation at 900–1100 °C for prolonged durations, cyclic oxidation (100 cycles at 1000 °C), adhesion (scratch testing), high‐temperature mechanical property measurements (hardness, elastic modulus, tensile strength), and comprehensive microstructural and compositional characterizations (XRD, SEM/EDS, TEM, FTIR, and XPS).
paper_reported: The Base Alloy exhibited a high mass gain (~15 mg/cm²) and a porous, multilayered oxide scale upon oxidation, while alloying with Cr, Co, and Mn (Synergy Alloy) led to a thinner, more continuous scale with a reduced parabolic oxidation rate constant (1.7 × 10⁻⁵ mg²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹) through the formation of an outer MnCr2O4 (and/or Cr2O3) layer and an inner Al2O3 layer.

Further addition of 0.5 at.% Y in the Innovation Alloy, fabricated by laser cladding, produced an ultra‐refined nanocrystalline structure and generated nanoscale (≈35 nm) Y2O3 particles that pinned the oxide scale, thereby reducing the oxidation rate constant three orders of magnitude to 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ mg²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹ and markedly improving scale adhesion (critical load of 78 N and interfacial fracture e

The study also reported enhanced high‐temperature mechanical performance (e.g., hardness of 310 HV, elastic modulus of 135 GPa, and tensile strength of 240 MPa at 1000 °C) and a higher apparent activation energy (~350 kJ/mol), establishing the effectiveness of a combined chemical and microstructural optimization strategy for designing protective high‐temperature coatings.
paper_proposed: That a triple‐synergistic framework integrating multi‐element alloying (specifically Cr, Co, Mn additions), trace reactive element modification (Y addition), and process‐induced nanocrystallization via laser cladding can serve as a novel paradigm for designing next‐generation, low‐cost, high‐performance protective coatings.

The approach emphasizes that combining compositional optimization with advanced processing routes enables the formation of a dense, duplex oxide scale (with an inner Al2O3 layer and an outer MnCr2O4/Cr2O3 layer) that is mechanically robust and thermodynamically stable under extreme high‐temperature conditions.

paper_did: Prepared three alloy systems: the Base Alloy (equiatomic FeNiCuAl), the Synergy Alloy (FeNiCuAl with 2.5 at.% each Cr, Co, and Mn), and the Innovation Alloy (Synergy Alloy with an additional 0.5 at.% Y) using arc melting and laser cladding.

Subjected the alloys to isothermal oxidation tests at 900 °C, 1000 °C, and 1100 °C (and cyclic oxidation at 1000 °C), with mass change measurements, adhesion (scratch) testing, and high‐temperature mechanical property evaluation.

Characterized the oxide scales and substrates by XRD, FTIR, XPS, SEM/EDS, and TEM to reveal that the Innovation Alloy forms a dense, duplex (MnCr2O4/Al2O3) oxide scale with nanoscale Y2O3 particles anchoring the interface.

Attributed enhanced oxidation resistance to a triple-synergy mechanism that integrates multi-element alloying (Cr, Co, Mn), trace reactive element (Y) addition, and laser-cladding-induced nanocrystallization.
paper_reported: The Base Alloy exhibits a high oxidation rate (mass gain ≈15 mg/cm2 and a high parabolic rate constant) with a thick, porous, heterogeneous oxide scale.
The Synergy Alloy shows improved oxidation resistance with the formation of a protective multilayer oxide scale, lowering the parabolic rate constant to 1.7 × 10−5 mg2·cm−4·s−1.

The Innovation Alloy achieves a dramatic three-order-of-magnitude reduction in oxidation rate (kp = 1.7 × 10−6 mg2·cm−4·s−1), a notably thinner oxide scale (~450 nm), enhanced oxide adhesion (critical load 78 N, interfacial fracture energy 14.8 J/m2), and maintains superior high-temperature mechanical performance.
paper_proposed: A design strategy for next-generation high-temperature protective coatings based on the synergistic coupling of chemical alloying and process-induced microstructural refinement.
A framework that could be extended for scalable low-cost, high-performance coatings through further chemical and processing optimizations.

hypotheses.conditions: Compare samples receiving the pre-anneal treatment with untreated baseline samples. Following the pre-treatment, expose both sets to prolonged exposure (e.g., 120 h) at 900–1100 °C under oxidizing gas and, in a separate set, under reducing conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin surface layer with reduced Ti concentration that shifts the oxidation chemistry so that Al and Cr primarily form the protective oxide scale.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under moderately reducing conditions, Ti—which tends to form less-protective, porous oxides—is encouraged to diffuse to the surface and segregate where it may volatilize or be preferentially removed (via reactions favored under reducing conditions). hypotheses.boundary: The pre-treatment must be optimized (temperature, time, and reducing gas partial pressure) to selectively affect the surface without altering the bulk nanocrystalline structure or degrading the overall mechanical performance; applicable for exposure temperatures between 900 and 1100 °C.
hypotheses.uncertainty: It is uncertain how effectively a short reducing heat treatment can deplete Ti from only the surface layers without impacting other beneficial diffusion pathways; the exact pre-treatment parameters require experimental optimization.

paper_did: Synthesized equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy and an alloy variant with approximately 6 at.% Al (with Mn reduced accordingly) using arc melting, casting, cold rolling, and recrystallization.
Subjected polished samples to controlled oxidation at 400°C in a 10 mbar O2 environment for time periods ranging from 2 to 120 minutes.

Used in situ atom probe tomography (APT), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) to monitor and analyze the evolution of oxide scales on the alloy surfaces.

Demonstrated the formation of layered oxides, including a Ni-enriched sublayer, a Cr-rich inner oxide, and outer oxides that are enriched in Fe, Mn, and Co, with non-uniformity in the outer scale and complex element-specific diffusion phenomena explained via the preferential interactivity parameter (PIP).
paper_reported: A detailed progression of oxidation was observed where early oxidation is dominated by fast oxidizers (e.g., Cr and Mn) due to their redox potentials and atomic sizes, leading to rapid formation of an initial oxide layer.

A layered oxide structure was reported—with an initial Ni-rich enrichment near the metal–oxide interface, followed by a Cr-rich inner oxide and an outer oxide that shows segregated regions (Fe, Co, Mn, and in the Al-added alloy, also Al) that evolve as oxidation continues.

Mechanistic insights were provided by relating atomic-scale behavior and diffusion kinetics (e.g., by comparing atomic radius, cohesive energy density, and standard reduction potentials) to the formation, speciation, and non-uniform architecture of surface oxides.
The study proposed that understanding these compositional and kinetic factors through methods like the PIP can lead to predictive design of complex alloys with improved oxidation resistance.
paper_proposed: The work is positioned to enable predictive alloy design for enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance by elucidating the fundamental oxidation mechanisms in high entropy alloys.

It suggests that leveraging the relationships between alloying elements’ thermodynamics and kinetics (through PIP and related parameters) will pave the way for future studies and alloy formulations that tailor oxidation behavior, although no specific post-processing or alternative exposure conditions were experimentally introduced in this study.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Degradation during elevated-temperature exposure is governed by the preferential, rapid oxidation of titanium at the alloy surface, forming a brittle Ti-rich oxide (likely TiO2) that creates a high-lattice-mismatch interface with the fcc matrix. This in turn induces stress and microcracking, which in oxidizing gases accelerates scale spallation and degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 exhibiting a single-phase FCC matrix with a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled post-build sub-transus heat treatment (at a moderate temperature below transformation onset) aimed at homogenizing Ti distribution and moderating the initial surface oxidation behavior.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose the treated and untreated samples at elevated temperature (e.g. 400°C) in oxidizing atmospheres (e.g. 10 mbar O2) for a fixed time (e.g. 120 min) with in situ monitoring of oxide scale development.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a Ti-rich oxide layer with a significant lattice mismatch relative to the underlying fcc matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: Due to titanium’s lower redox potential and its relatively high diffusivity in the alloy, Ti oxidizes first to form TiO2. Because TiO2 has different lattice parameters and mechanical properties relative to the FCC matrix (similar to the observed early oxidation kinetics and strain effects for fast-oxidizers in the paper, see PMC11169556::web::006 and ::007), this leads to interfacial stresses that promote microcracking. These cracks then act as fast diffusion paths for further oxidation and scale spallation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The untreated alloy will show early onset of TiO2 formation, crack nucleation, and spallation of the oxide scale, whereas the heat-treated alloy with improved Ti distribution will exhibit a more gradual oxide formation and less degradation. The magnitude of improvement may be moderate, but clearly discernible by reduced crack density and lower oxidation rates.
hypotheses.baseline: Behavior of the as-built alloy undergoing oxidation without prior heat treatment.
hypotheses.boundary: This hypothesis applies for oxidation conditions at moderate temperatures (around 400°C) where oxide scale formation is diffusion-controlled, and the fcc matrix remains stable.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative estimates of stress and crack density are difficult to predict precisely; however, the trend should be observable.

hypotheses.intervention: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation annealing step in a mildly reducing atmosphere (e.g. a H2/Ar mixture at 350–400°C for a brief period) to induce surface segregation of Cr and Al before full oxidizing or reducing exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: After the pre-treatment, expose the samples to elevated temperature (e.g. 400°C) in either an oxidizing (O2-rich) or a reducing (H2-containing) gas environment. Compare with samples not receiving the pre-treatment.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Development of a Cr–Al rich surface layer and subsequent formation of a dense Cr2O3/Al2O3 mixed oxide scale.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-treatment in a mildly reducing environment facilitates the migration of Cr and Al to the surface (analogous to the element segregation phenomena predicted by PIP in the paper, see PMC11169556::web::003 and ::009). This enriched layer rapidly forms a protective oxide upon subsequent exposure. By suppressing the premature oxidation of Ti (which can form a less coherent oxide), the alloy develops a more stable, adherent oxide scale that impedes further diffusion of oxygen or reductants, thereby mitigating degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The pre-treated samples will exhibit significantly lower degradation rates, as evidenced by reduced oxide thickness growth rates and fewer spallation events compared to untreated ones. The protective oxide will be compositionally richer in Cr and Al.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated additively manufactured samples exposed directly to oxidizing or reducing gases at high temperature.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism applies to exposure conditions where the oxidation-reduction reactions are surface diffusion-limited (typically at moderate temperatures around 400°C) and does not induce phase change in the FCC matrix.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact degree of improvement is hard to forecast quantitatively, but the trend in oxide integrity should be observable.

hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism applies to conditions where the microstructural effects and residual stress dominate the oxidation kinetics, typically at moderate temperatures (~400°C) before any bulk phase transformations occur.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement is subject to processing parameters and may vary; however, the qualitative trend of enhanced oxide uniformity is expected.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Protective oxide scale formation from selective oxidation of Al and Cr governs degradation under oxidizing conditions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix and a relatively pristine surface.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to develop a continuous, dual-layer oxide scale enriched in Al2O3 and Cr2O3 before subjecting samples to prolonged high-temperature oxidizing exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) in controlled oxidizing gas environments (with defined oxygen partial pressure) for defined exposure durations.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A protective, adherent oxide scale that forms heterogeneously yet continuously on the alloy surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: At high temperatures, the inherent presence of aluminum and chromium promotes selective oxidation to form a composite oxide scale. This scale, by virtue of its low ionic diffusivity and excellent adhesion, impedes further oxygen ingress. In oxidizing environments, the integrity of this scale slows down further degradation. Under reducing conditions, however, the scale’s composition can change or be partially reduced, diminishing its protectiveness. Thus, the scale’s nature and adherence govern the long-term stability of the alloy without compromising the FCC matrix’s mechanical integrity.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit lower weight gain and reduced oxide scale thickening vs. non-treated samples when exposed to oxidizing high-temperature environments. A substantial protective effect (direction: improvement in oxidation resistance) is expected, although the precise magnitude is moderately uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Degradation behavior of as-built, untreated alloy surfaces under similar exposures.
hypotheses.boundary: Effectiveness is expected only in environments with sufficiently high oxygen partial pressures and temperatures where selective oxidation is active; in reducing atmospheres the beneficial oxide may be compromised.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Moderate uncertainty exists in scale adhesion variations and potential scale spallation effects at the upper end of the temperature range.

In fine-grained samples, the higher grain boundary area enhances oxygen transport into the bulk, promoting internal oxidation and the formation of subsurface oxide networks. This internal oxidation undermines the structural integrity over time. The contrast between fine-grained and coarse-grained samples should reveal the role of grain boundary diffusion in degradation.

paper_did: Manufactured Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 high entropy alloy samples via selective electron beam melting (SEBM) from a blended elemental powder mix using a modified small-scale powder delivery system.
Performed post-manufacturing vacuum heat treatments at 1000 °C and 1300 °C to promote microstructural homogenization despite non‐optimized process parameters.

Characterized the as-built and heat-treated samples by SEM/EPMA and X‐ray diffraction, identifying two solid solution phases (an Al‐poor TaMoNb-based matrix and a minor Al‐rich (TaMoNbCr)Al phase) and recording significant residual porosity.
Documented notable evaporation of light elements (especially Al and Cr) during both the SEBM process and subsequent heat treatments.
paper_reported: That in situ alloying from a blended elemental powder mix is achievable via SEBM, forming a dual-phase microstructure rather than a single high–configurational entropy phase.
The as-built alloy exhibits a heterogeneous distribution of Al (with a matrix phase low in Al and a secondary phase enriched in Al) alongside significant residual porosity.
Post-manufacturing heat treatments improve microstructural homogenization but also lead to further depletion of key alloying elements such as Al and Cr.
paper_proposed: Future work should focus on optimizing the process parameters of SEBM (rather than relying on heat treatments) to reduce residual porosity and better control the alloy composition.
Further development in the in situ alloying approach is needed to achieve a more homogeneous microstructure in refractory high entropy alloys produced from elemental powder blends.

paper_did: Manufactured an Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 high‐entropy alloy via selective electron beam melting (SEBM) using a mechanically blended elemental powder feedstock.

Employed a modified SEBM setup (with a vertical powder container and small batch handling) and processed the samples using specified beam parameters (e.g. 80 mm/s, 20 mA) without parameter optimization.
Performed post‐manufacturing vacuum heat treatments at 1000 °C and 1300 °C to examine their effects on microstructural homogenization while characterizing the samples by SEM/EPMA and XRD.
paper_reported: In‐situ alloying was achieved despite significant elemental evaporation, notably of Al, as evidenced by the as‐built sample containing only about 8.4 at.% Al versus the intended 12 at.%.
The resulting microstructure consisted of two distinct solid solutions: a majority Al‐poor BCC matrix (TaMoNb‐based solid solution) and a minor Al‐rich phase ((TaMoNbCr)Al solid solution).

Residual porosity remained high in all samples, and while heat treatments improved microstructural homogenization, they did not reduce the porosity and further promoted compositional depletion (additional loss of Al and Cr).
paper_proposed: The study suggests that further work should focus on process parameter optimization (rather than solely relying on post‐process heat treatments) to reduce porosity and better control evaporation losses during SEBM processing of high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Compensatory Doping to Offset Evaporative Losses for Improved Protective Oxide Scale Formation
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix produced by additive manufacturing using nominal elemental ratios.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the initial powder feedstock by adding approximately 5 at.% extra Al (and/or a modest extra amount of Cr if needed) relative to the nominal design to compensate for evaporation losses during processing.
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere (such as air or a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A sustained availability of protective elements at the alloy’s surface that fosters the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (predominantly Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃).
hypotheses.mechanism: During the SEBM process it has been observed that significant evaporation of light elements (notably Al) occurs. This evaporation may lead to locally depleted concentrations of Al (and possibly Cr), which are critical to forming a protective oxide barrier. By pre-emptively adding extra Al to the powder blend, after processing the surface retains sufficient Al to form a uniform and adherent oxide layer. The improved oxide scale serves as a barrier to further oxygen ingress during high-temperature exposure, thereby mitigating oxidation-induced degradation while preserving the fcc matrix and mechanical integrity.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the compensatory-doped samples should exhibit lower weight gain during oxidation tests, a more uniform and continuous oxide scale (as confirmed by SEM/EPMA), and fewer spallation features.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-built HEA produced with the nominal composition (without compensatory doping), which is susceptible to elemental depletion by evaporation.
hypotheses.boundary: This improvement is expected to be significant under oxidizing conditions; under reducing conditions, where oxide formation is minimal, the effect may be less pronounced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal extra doping level is uncertain and may require refinement; interactions between extra Al and other elements in the fcc matrix need to be monitored to ensure mechanical properties remain uncompromised.

hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small addition (approximately 0.5–1 at.%) of hafnium (Hf) into the elemental powder blend during the additive manufacturing process.
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) under both oxidizing and moderately reducing gas environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of Hf-rich precipitates near grain boundaries and at internal interfaces that act to pin microstructural defects and modify local oxidation kinetics.
hypotheses.mechanism: Hafnium has a high oxygen affinity and forms stable, finely dispersed HfO₂ particles when exposed to oxygen. By incorporating a minor amount of Hf, these particles can preferentially form at sites that would otherwise serve as active regions for rapid oxidation initiation (such as nano-precipitates or inclusions). The presence of stable HfO₂ can act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion and reduce the formation of non-uniform oxide regions, thereby mitigating localized degradation without significantly altering the bulk fcc microstructure.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Hf-doped samples should show a more uniform oxide scale with reduced spallation, lower overall oxidation-induced weight gain, and fewer localized degradation sites compared to undoped controls, particularly under oxidizing conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: As-built HEA without any Hf addition, potentially exhibiting heterogeneous oxide nucleation from existing inclusions or precipitates.
hypotheses.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated under oxidizing conditions where Hf can form stable oxides; under purely reducing conditions the impact might be minimal, and care must be taken to maintain overall mechanical performance.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise effective concentration of Hf and its distribution within the microstructure remain to be optimized, and possible interactions with other alloying elements need careful monitoring.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Laser-Induced Graded Near-Surface Microstructure to Alleviate Thermal Mismatch Stresses and Oxide Spallation
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix produced by additive manufacturing, featuring a relatively uniform near-surface grain structure.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a targeted laser surface remelting post-processing treatment to create a graded microstructure in the near-surface region, with a finer grain structure at the extreme surface transitioning to coarser grains in the underlying bulk.
hypotheses.conditions: Post-treated samples are subsequently exposed to elevated-temperature environments (700–900 °C) under oxidizing conditions (and optionally under reducing conditions) with thermal cycling.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A graded microstructure that moderates the elastic mismatch between the oxide scale and the substrate, reducing residual stresses at the metal/oxide interface.
hypotheses.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, differential thermal expansion between the alloy substrate and the growing oxide scale can lead to stress accumulation and subsequent scale spallation. By engineering a graded microstructure via laser surface remelting, the near-surface region attains a gradient in grain size whereby a very fine surface layer can better accommodate strain while the coarser sub-surface retains bulk strength. This gradation alleviates thermal mismatch stresses at the interface, leading to a more adherent oxide scale and lower degradation rates.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples with a graded near-surface microstructure should exhibit reduced oxide scale spallation (as evidenced by lower weight gain and higher scale adhesion), compared to untreated samples. The graded approach is expected to maintain mechanical integrity while improving oxidation resistance under cyclic thermal conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: As-built HEA with a homogenous near-surface grain structure obtained via standard SEBM processing.
hypotheses.boundary: This strategy is particularly beneficial under conditions of thermal cycling in oxidizing environments; under steady-state reducing conditions, the effect is anticipated to be less significant.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal laser remelting parameters and resulting gradient profile need fine-tuning to avoid compromising fatigue performance, and the extent of reduction in mismatch stresses is subject to experimental validation.

paper_did: Fabricated thin‐walled high‐entropy alloy specimens using plasma arc additive manufacturing with a 50‐layer deposition on a 316L stainless steel substrate.

Processed the AlCoCrFeNi2 alloy powder using a plasma arc oscillation process with robotic reciprocation and a zigzag layer‐by‐layer scanning pattern under defined parameters (e.g., 120 A current, specific gas flows, interlayer cooling).

Characterized the resultant samples by optical/SEM metallography, Vickers hardness profiling across the deposit (revealing a gradient from bottom to top), and tensile testing in both longitudinal and transverse directions to evaluate mechanical anisotropy and microstructural evolution.
paper_reported: The microstructure consists of dendritic and columnar crystals with a dual-phase FCC+BCC composition that evolves with deposition height and thermal cycling.
There is a hardness gradient – with higher Vickers microhardness observed in the upper regions – correlated with grain refinement and microstructural regularity.

Tensile tests indicated significant differences between longitudinal (better ductility and consistent strength) and transverse specimens, with the additive process inducing anisotropy due to preferential grain alignment and residual thermal gradients.
The study discussed how thermal cycles during deposition affect grain size, elemental distribution, and the evolution of phases as a function of sedimentary height.
paper_proposed: Future research will focus on enhancing the adaptability of plasma arc–fabricated high‐entropy alloys to extreme environments, improving process economy, and tailoring microstructural functionality for industrial applications in areas such as aerospace and nuclear energy.
There is an intent to advance material innovations and technological breakthroughs so that high‐quality HEAs can move from laboratory-scale experiments to strategic industrial applications.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Under oxidizing conditions, degradation of the additively manufactured alloy is governed by the formation and eventual breakdown of a duplex oxide scale, where an inner Al-rich (and partly Cr-rich) protective oxide and an outer less-protective oxide develop at the surface. The degradation rate is controlled by the rate at which alloying elements diffuse from the matrix (especially via grain boundaries) to sustain the oxide scale.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix produced by plasma arc additive manufacturing, exhibiting a dendritic/columnar microstructure with moderate grain size.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a post-build annealing step designed to refine and homogenize the grain size (promoting a fine-grained microstructure) without altering the overall phase (still FCC).
hypotheses.conditions: Expose samples to a controlled oxidizing gas environment at elevated temperatures (within the regime where oxidation is significant but below melting) and compare as-built versus annealed samples.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density and uniformity of element distribution.
hypotheses.mechanism: A fine-grained microstructure increases the density of fast diffusion paths (grain boundaries) that facilitate a more uniform supply of Al and Cr to the surface. This leads to the formation of a coherent, continuous, and adherent protective inner oxide layer (Al2O3/Cr2O3 mix). In the as‐built or coarser-grained condition, less uniform diffusion results in regions where the protective scale is starved for Al/Cr, leading to scale breakdown and accelerated oxidation degradation. This mechanism builds on the concept of elemental diffusion influencing oxide scale stability, noted indirectly in the discussion of microstructure-driven mechanical properties in the paper (e.g., PMC12843301::web::015, PMC12843301::web::018).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Annealed (fine-grained) samples will exhibit slower scale growth rates, lower oxide spallation, and reduced mass gain/loss over time compared with the as-built baseline. The improvement is expected to be moderate based on typical diffusion-controlled oxidation effects (exact quantitative improvement uncertain due to complex synergistic effects).
hypotheses.baseline: The original as-built alloy with its typical dendritic/columnar morphology and moderate grain size.
hypotheses.boundary: Test temperatures should be high enough to promote oxidation (e.g., 600–800 °C) and maintain the integrity of the FCC matrix; exposure times must be sufficient to form measurable oxide layers.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is uncertain due to the synergistic interplay of multiple elements in the HEA.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Under reducing gas exposure, degradation is controlled by selective internal oxidation at preferential sites (such as grain boundary triple junctions) driven by local elemental segregation. The depletion of Cr and Ti at these sites leads to microvoid formation and embrittlement.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix, which in the additive process may exhibit regions of elemental (Cr and Ti) segregation at grain boundaries.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a homogenization heat treatment below the melting point to reduce microsegregation while preserving the overall FCC matrix and mechanical integrity.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose both the as-built and homogenized samples to slightly reducing gas mixtures (e.g., a controlled mixture with a low oxygen partial pressure) at elevated temperatures where internal oxidation processes are activated.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Element segregation at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
hypotheses.mechanism: In reducing atmospheres, the limited availability of oxygen causes selective internal oxidation along regions already prone to elemental segregation (notably Cr and Ti), leading to the formation of non-protective oxide clusters and resulting microvoids. The homogenization treatment is expected to reduce such segregation, thereby lowering the propensity for internal oxidation-induced degradation. This mechanism is plausible given the interplay between processing-induced segregation and subsequent oxidation behavior (see microstructural observations in PMC12843301::web::013 and discussion in high-entropy alloy texts).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Homogenized samples will show fewer signs of internal oxidation (fewer microvoids, less embrittlement) and maintain mechanical integrity better than the as-built samples when exposed to reducing conditions. The reduction in degradation is anticipated to be noticeable but its exact magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-built alloy state with known localized segregation from the additive process.
hypotheses.boundary: Exposure in a reducing gas environment with controlled oxygen partial pressure (for example, a mixture of inert gas with trace oxygen) at temperatures relevant to service (e.g., 600–750 °C) and for durations sufficient to highlight internal oxidation differences.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The degree to which homogenization can mitigate segregation and consequently reduce internal oxidation needs to be established experimentally.

paper_did: Prepared a thin‐walled AlCoCrFeNi2 high‐entropy alloy (HEA) using plasma arc additive manufacturing with a 50‐layer deposition on a 316L stainless steel substrate.

Employed a plasma arc oscillation process with robotic reciprocation and layer‐by‐layer zigzag scanning, using controlled parameters (e.g., deposition current, gas flow rates, interlayer cooling) and PSPW-AICo1 alloy powder.

Fabricated test specimens for metallographic analysis, Vickers microhardness measurements (across the cross‐section and along the deposition direction), and tensile testing (both longitudinal and transverse) to assess microstructural evolution and anisotropic mechanical properties.
paper_reported: The deposited HEA displayed a dense, defect‐free dendritic microstructure with epitaxial columnar grains that varied with deposition height – the bottom showing coarse columnar and cellular dendrites and the upper layers showing refined, layered structures.
A gradient in Vickers microhardness was observed (hardness increasing from ~473 HV at the bottom to ~556 HV at the top), correlating with the grain refinement effect from repeated thermal cycles.

Tensile tests revealed anisotropy: longitudinal (parallel-to-deposition) specimens exhibited more regular microstructural arrangements and better ductility than transverse specimens, with strength and plasticity differences attributed to the underlying microstructural evolution.
paper_proposed: Future research should focus on optimizing plasma arc manufacturing for straight-arm high-entropy alloys by enhancing adaptability to extreme environments, improving process economy, and fine-tuning microstructural functionality.
Advancing the technology from laboratory-scale experiments toward industrial applications in strategic fields such as aerospace, nuclear energy, and energy sectors.

hypotheses.intervention: Apply a two-step heat treatment: (1) pre-oxidation in a mildly reducing atmosphere (low oxygen partial pressure, e.g., nitrogen with a trace of oxygen) at ~600 °C to form a sub-stoichiometric inner oxide, and (2) re-oxidation in synthetic air at ~650–700 °C to gradually mature the oxide scale.
hypotheses.conditions: After the dual-atmosphere pre-treatment, expose the samples to further elevated-temperature testing (650–750 °C) under both oxidizing and reducing gas conditions to monitor degradation behavior over time.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A duplex oxide scale comprising a dense, sub-stoichiometric inner layer (formed during the reducing pre-treatment) and an outer, fully oxidized layer, which together act as a robust barrier to oxygen ingress and mitigate local oxidation of reactive elements such as Ti.
hypotheses.mechanism: The sequential gas exposure tailors the oxide scale: the initial reducing treatment limits the formation of volatile Ti oxides and other non-protective phases by forming a thin, slightly oxygen-deficient oxide, while the subsequent oxidizing step densifies and stabilizes the scale. This duplex structure is anticipated to adhere better and slow further oxygen diffusion even under final oxidizing or reducing exposures, thus maintaining bulk mechanical integrity.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Dual pre-treated samples will show slower mass gain, a more adherent and uniform oxide scale, and reduced degradation (e.g., fewer signs of spallation or internal oxidation) compared to untreated as‐built samples. The exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain, as it depends on the precise control of pre-treatment atmospheres and durations.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated as‐built HEA samples that develop oxide scales directly under high-temperature exposure, possibly with less controlled scale morphology.
hypotheses.boundary: The pre-treatment temperatures (600–700 °C) and duration must remain low enough to avoid bulk microstructural changes and must be optimized to form the desired sub-stoichiometric oxide without initiating unwanted diffusion or phase transformations.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The sensitivity of the oxide scale properties to the exact dual-atmosphere parameters, and whether the duplex scale remains stable during prolonged service, are uncertain.

paper_did: Employed plasma arc additive manufacturing with a plasma arc oscillation process to fabricate 50‐layer, thin‐walled high‐entropy alloy samples (AlCoCrFeNi2) on a 316L stainless steel substrate.
Utilized a reciprocating, layer‐by‐layer deposition with well‐defined parameters (e.g., plasma current, gas flow rates, interlayer cooling, layer height) to form a stable deposit.

Prepared specimens by cutting the as‐built deposit and performing metallographic analyses (SEM imaging), hardness measurements (Vickers microhardness along different regions), and tensile tests on both longitudinal (parallel) and transverse (perpendicular) orientations.
paper_reported: A clear, dendritic microstructure with columnar and intergranular features was observed, with a dual-phase (FCC+BCC) structure evolving from bottom to top due to differing thermal cycles.
A hardness gradient was recorded: microhardness increased from about 473 HV at the bottom to about 556 HV at the top, attributed to grain refinement and phase transformations.

Tensile tests showed that longitudinal specimens (parallel to the deposition direction) exhibited more regular structures and higher ductility compared to transverse specimens, which suffered from stress concentration effects.
paper_proposed: Future work should address scalability and industrial applicability by enhancing adaptability to extreme environments, improving process economy, and tailoring microstructural functionality.
The paper points toward further research in optimizing plasma arc processing for high‐quality high‐entropy alloys, with targeted applications in aerospace, nuclear, and energy sectors.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: As‐built, plasma arc–fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix and dendritic/columnar microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the alloy to a series of short, high‐temperature cycles (e.g., 5 minutes at ~750 °C followed by rapid cooling) in an inert or low‐oxygen atmosphere before exposure to service conditions.
hypotheses.conditions: Cycles performed in an inert gas (e.g., high-purity argon) followed by subsequent exposure at 650–750 °C in oxidizing (synthetic air) or reducing gas environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enrichment of Cr and Al in the near‐surface region due to differential diffusivities during rapid thermal cycling.
hypotheses.mechanism: During the brief high-temperature pulses, elements with higher mobility—specifically Cr and Al—migrate preferentially to the surface. This enriched layer then, upon subsequent high‐temperature exposure, forms a thin, adherent Cr/Al‐rich oxide that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and further degradation. This approach leverages kinetic differences in the multicomponent system without triggering bulk phase changes.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to as‐built samples, thermally pre‐treated specimens will exhibit a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale with lower mass gain, thereby slowing the degradation rate. hypotheses.baseline: The as‐built HEA that, when exposed directly, develops a less controlled oxide scale with potential spallation or nonuniform growth due to its inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
hypotheses.boundary: Thermal cycle peak temperatures (around 750 °C) and durations must be optimized to induce surface segregation without altering the FCC bulk microstructure or causing unwanted phase transformations.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimum cycle number, duration, and temperature are uncertain and require experimental calibration to ensure effective surface enrichment without deleterious effects.

hypotheses.mechanism: The rapid solidification associated with laser remelting homogenizes and refines the surface microstructure. This transient high-energy process promotes the segregation of passivating elements toward the extreme surface. During subsequent high-temperature exposure, this graded zone evolves into a duplex oxide scale with a dense inner layer that limits oxygen diffusion and an outer layer that adjusts to environmental changes, thus mitigating degradation.

hypotheses.boundary: Laser treatment parameters (energy, pulse duration, remelting depth) must be precisely controlled to affect only the surface without compromising the bulk microstructure or mechanical properties.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal laser parameters and exact graded oxide scale structure are uncertain; pilot experiments are needed to establish processing windows.

paper_did: Synthesized a refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 alloy via arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Conducted isothermal oxidation tests in static air at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h and at 900 °C for 50 h, with repeated mass measurements.
Characterized the oxide scale evolution by X‐ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), including cross‐sectional analyses.
paper_reported: At 600–700 °C, a two‐stage oxidation kinetics was observed: an initial nearly parabolic (n ≃ 0.46–0.48) stage transitioning to a faster, breakaway oxidation stage (n ≃ 0.72–0.75), attributed to cracking/spallation induced by the formation of voluminous Nb2O5 and TiNb2O7 oxides and, at 700 °C, to partial evaporation of V2O5.

At 800 °C, oxidation followed nearly linear kinetics (n ≃ 0.92) due to the rapid formation of a porous and unprotective scale composed mainly of complex oxides (TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, Nb2Zr6O17), while at 900 °C the specimen disintegrated.
The study identified the key role of volatile V‐rich oxides and the subsequent evolution of complex oxide scales in governing oxidation degradation.
paper_proposed: Improving oxidation resistance by modifying the alloy’s chemical composition—such as reducing elements (e.g., V, Ti) responsible for unprotective oxides or adding elements (Al, Cr, Si) known to form stronger, protective scales.
Considering protective coatings as an alternative route for enhancing high-temperature oxidation performance.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Post‐processing grain growth in the additively manufactured alloy reduces high-angle grain boundary density, thus mitigating rapid oxygen ingress through intergranular paths that initiate scale cracking and degradation during elevated-temperature exposure in oxidizing atmospheres.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a fine-scale, non-equilibrium microstructure typical of additive manufacturing.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled high-temperature annealing (subsolidus, e.g., 900–950 °C for several hours) to promote modest grain growth and reduce high-energy intergranular defects without inducing unwanted phase transformations.
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 700–800 °C) in an oxidizing gas environment (static air) for durations comparable to service conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Reduced density of fast diffusion paths (grain boundaries) leading to a more continuous and adherent oxide layer with lower porosity.
hypotheses.mechanism: Coarser grains lead to fewer grain boundary channels for oxygen diffusion. With reduced oxygen ingress, formation of unprotective or volatile oxides (e.g., transient Cr or Ti oxides) is minimized and the protective oxide scale remains intact. This effect builds on the paper’s identification of scale cracking and oxygen ingress through defects as degradation triggers.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A lower mass gain per unit area and a more coherent, less porous oxide scale compared to the as-built condition, with a reduction in scale spallation evident over similar exposure times. The improvement is expected to be moderate but significant under the chosen exposure conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-built alloy exhibiting a fine, high defect density microstructure leading to faster degradation as evidenced by the evolution of porosity and spallation under oxidation (akin to crack propagation observed in the refractory HEA studied in the paper).
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention should not be so severe as to coarsen grains excessively or promote undesirable phase transformations that compromise the alloy’s overall mechanical integrity.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is uncertain because the optimal balance between grain size and mechanical properties must be calibrated.

paper_did: Developed ultrafine‐grained microstructures in AlCoCrFeNi HEA by applying stationary friction processing (SFP) at two rotational speeds (400 and 1800 rpm) to an as‐cast alloy with coarse (~100 μm) grains.

Characterized microstructural changes including dynamic recrystallization, phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC, increased defect density, compressive residual stresses, and elevated surface free energy.

Conducted high‐temperature oxidation tests in the range of 850–1050 °C for 100 hours, quantifying oxidation kinetics (mass gain, parabolic rate constants) and correlating them with the refined grain structure.

Identified distinct oxide scale formations where processed samples primarily formed protective Cr2O3 and Al-rich (alumina) layers, in contrast to the as‐cast alloy which developed mixed, cracked, and nonprotective spinel oxides.
paper_reported: The refined (ultrafine-grained) microstructure markedly reduces the oxidation kinetics—with reported reductions in mass gain of 12–20% (SFP_400) and 38–48% (SFP_1800)—as compared to the as-cast state.

Enhanced oxidation resistance is attributed to the increased grain boundary density and higher surface free energy that promote rapid short-circuit diffusion of Cr and Al, leading to the formation of a dense, adherent, protective oxide scale (chromia topped by Al-rich inner oxides).
The processed samples also exhibit higher activation energies and thinner oxide scales, confirming that the microstructural modifications play a crucial role in retarding oxidation.
paper_proposed: That tailoring the microstructure via severe plastic deformation (here by SFP) can significantly improve high-temperature oxidation resistance in HEAs by controlling the nature and adherence of the oxide scale.
An implicit suggestion to explore further microstructural refinement approaches as a new route to modulate oxidation behavior in high-entropy alloys.

Performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations using VASP to optimize structures and determine elastic constants and mechanical properties, and used OLCAO to analyze electronic structure, calculate bond orders, partial charges, and derive total bond order density (TBOD).

Computed thermodynamic parameters (ΔSmix, ΔHmix, ΔGmix, Ω, atomic size difference δ, VEC, electronegativity differences) to assess phase stability and predict formation of single-phase solid solutions versus secondary phases.

Investigated the influence of lattice distortion on interatomic bond distributions (bond order vs. bond length), and correlated these bonding characteristics with mechanical (elastic moduli, hardness) and thermal properties.

Demonstrated that models with smaller lattice distortions (e.g., model m6) exhibit higher TBOD and more uniform bonding, suggesting enhanced cohesion and stability compared to models with broader bond length distributions (e.g., m1).

Showed quantitative correlations between lattice distortion, interatomic bonding (via TBOD), and macroscopic mechanical/thermal properties, thereby providing potential descriptors for guiding future alloy design.
paper_proposed: Suggested that the insights gained from the computational correlations between TBOD, lattice distortion, and overall stability could inform strategies to design new RHEAs with tailored properties.

Proposed that future experimental and computational efforts can leverage these bonding and lattice distortion metrics to modify compositions or processing routes for improved performance in high-temperature applications.

paper_did: Performed DFT calculations using VASP and OLCAO on six refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) models composed of nine refractory elements (Ti, V, Cr, Zr, Nb, Mo, Hf, Ta, W) with varying elemental ratios.
Calculated phase stability parameters (ΔSmix, ΔHmix, ΔGmix, Ω, δ, ∧) to assess the likelihood of forming single‐phase BCC solid solutions versus secondary phases.
Investigated the electronic structure through total and partial density of states (DOS/PDOS) analyses, correlating N(EF) with predicted electrical conductivity.

paper_reported: Reported that variations in elemental composition significantly affect phase stability and may lead to the formation of single-phase BCC solid solutions or secondary phases, as indicated by parameters like Ω, δ, and the ∧ parameter.

Demonstrated that differences in the electronic density of states at the Fermi level among the models forecast variations in conductivity, while the bonding and elastic property calculations offer insights into the internal cohesion of the alloys.
paper_proposed: Proposed that the computational insights on the interplay between lattice distortion, interatomic bonding (TBOD), and mechanical/thermal properties can guide the tailored design of refractory HEAs for high‐temperature applications.

Suggested that the correlations observed between microstructural (bonding, charge distribution) and macroscopic properties (elastic moduli, thermal properties) in these RHEAs might inform future experimental validations and the design of novel alloys.

Employed first-principles DFT calculations (using VASP for structural and mechanical properties and OLCAO for electronic structure and interatomic bonding) on large supercells to simulate disordered BCC solid solutions.

Calculated and analyzed thermodynamic parameters (ΔSmix, ΔHmix, ΔGmix, Ω, δ, VEC, Δχ), electronic density of states (DOS/PDOS), partial charges, bond orders, and total bond order density (TBOD) to elucidate phase stability, lattice distortion, and interatomic cohesion.

Determined elastic constants and derived mechanical moduli using a stress–strain approach, then correlated lattice distortion (via bond-order vs bond-length distributions and charge scattering) with mechanical and thermal properties.
paper_reported: Revealed that variations in elemental ratios dramatically affect the electronic structure (e.g., variations in TDOS at the Fermi level) and the nature of interatomic bonding in RHEAs.

Showed that models with higher lattice distortion (as evidenced from a more scattered bond-order vs bond-length distribution and elevated partial charge activity) correlate with lower total bond order density and modified mechanical properties.

Presented computed elastic properties (bulk, shear, and Young’s moduli, hardness, etc.) and demonstrated how subtle changes in atomic arrangement and bonding metrics impact the material’s strength, ductility, and thermal behavior.

Identified that thermodynamic and chemical factors (such as high Ω but large δ and electronegativity differences) predict a predominance of BCC solid solution with possible secondary phases, guiding future experimental and computational investigations.
paper_proposed: Encouraged future experimental validations and computational explorations on how subtle compositional variations and associated lattice distortions impact mechanical performance and thermal stability.

hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a minor addition (≈0.5 at%) of boron (B) into the powder feedstock used for additive manufacturing to achieve in situ segregation of boron to grain boundaries during solidification.
hypotheses.conditions: Fabricate two sets of samples from the same process: one with the 0.5 at% B microalloying and one without (baseline). After fabrication, subject both to high-temperature exposure (≈900 °C for 50–100 hours) under both oxidizing (air) and reducing (H2/N2) atmospheres.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Preferential segregation of boron at grain boundaries increases local covalent bonding character and enhances the total bond order density (TBOD) at these critical regions, thereby reducing the connectivity of fast-diffusion paths for oxygen or reducing species.
hypotheses.mechanism: Drawing on the paper’s detailed analysis that links local variations in bond order and electronic structure with lattice distortions (PMC11748199::web::017::partial_charge_and_interatomic_bonding_c), the small B addition is expected to concentrate at high-energy grain boundaries where it can form stronger bonds. This enhancement in bond order at the interfaces should impede the mobility of reactive species by reinforcing intergranular cohesion without altering the bulk FCC matrix responsible for strength and fatigue performance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: B-doped samples will show improved degradation resistance during both oxidizing and reducing high-temperature exposures, such as reduced weight change, a more coherent and adherent surface scale, and fewer microstructural defects (e.g., voids or cracks) at grain boundaries relative to the undoped baseline. Precise effect sizes are uncertain until quantified.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard AM alloy without B addition, which exhibits inherent intergranular lattice distortion that facilitates rapid diffusion of reactive species and subsequent degradation.
hypotheses.boundary: The B concentration must remain very low (≈0.5 at%) to ensure that it segregates at the grain boundaries rather than forming a secondary phase in the bulk, which would risk compromising the alloy’s mechanical integrity.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative effect of the enhanced intergranular TBOD due to B segregation on degradation kinetics needs to be established; while the mechanistic basis is supported, specific scales of improvement are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AM specimens from identical batches: one with 0.5 at% boron addition and one without. Characterize grain-boundary chemistry (using APT or TEM/EDS) to confirm B segregation and measure local TBOD variations. Then expose both sets at 900 °C for 50–100 hours in oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. Assess degradation via weight change, oxide scale morphology (SEM, XPS), and intergranular microstructure analysis.
measurements: APT/TEM-EDS for boron segregation and intergranular TBOD
Gravimetric analysis for weight change
SEM/XPS for surface scale and microstructural integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the B-microalloyed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in degradation resistance (e.g., similar weight changes, oxide scale disintegration, or unchanged grain-boundary characteristics) compared to the baseline, or if no significant B segregation is detected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

paper_did: Developed atomistic models of six refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) composed of nine elements (Ti, V, Cr, Zr, Nb, Mo, Hf, Ta, and W) using an 8×8×8 BCC supercell containing 1024 atoms.

Performed DFT calculations (using VASP for structural optimization and OLCAO for electronic structure and interatomic bonding analysis) to compute phase stability parameters (ΔSmix, ΔHmix, ΔGmix, Ω, δ, VEC, etc.), elastic constants, and mechanical moduli.

Analyzed the electronic structure via density‐of-states (DOS) and partial DOS, quantified bonding via bond order (BO) and partial charges (PC and Q*), and extracted the total bond order density (TBOD) as a measure of internal cohesion and lattice distortion.

Explored how variations in elemental ratios affect lattice distortion, mechanical properties, and thermal properties, thereby linking local bond order heterogeneity and charge distribution scattering with the materials’ fast diffusion channels.
paper_reported: Evidence that different elemental distributions lead to variations in lattice distortion, with models like m1 showing broader spread in bond-order versus bond-length (indicative of higher distortion) and m6 exhibiting a more concentrated PBOD and higher TBOD.

Correlations between electronic features (such as DOS minima near the Fermi level), elastic properties, and the degree of local bonding heterogeneity, suggesting that lattice distortion plays a key role in governing mechanical and degradation-related properties.

The potential influence of atomic-scale interactions (e.g., local bond order density, partial charge scattering) on overall phase stability, mechanical integrity, and diffusion processes in these complex alloys.
paper_proposed: Further exploration of how varying elemental compositions can be used to deliberately control lattice distortion and, consequently, properties such as strength, ductility, and thermal stability in RHEAs.

Experimental and computational follow‐up studies to validate the predicted correlations between interatomic bonding metrics (like TBOD and PBOD) and macroscopic properties, opening avenues for tailored alloy design.

hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small amount (~1 at%) Si into the feedstock during additive manufacturing to promote in situ segregation of Si to grain boundaries.
hypotheses.conditions: Process a set of samples with the Si microalloying and use an otherwise identical AM process. Post-fabrication, subject both Si-doped and undoped samples to elevated-temperature exposure (≈900 °C for 50–100 hours) under both oxidizing (air) and reducing (controlled H2/N2 mixtures) atmospheres.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced local intergranular bond order density via formation of Si-O or Si-metal bonds at grain boundaries, leading to a more chemically passivated, structurally cohesive interface that impedes fast-diffusion pathways.
hypotheses.mechanism: Building on the DFT findings that link local bond order heterogeneity with regions of high lattice distortion (PMC11748199::web::017::partial_charge_and_interatomic_bonding_c), the added Si is expected to segregate to the high-energy grain boundaries. There, it should form stronger bonds (or a very thin, protective silicate-type layer) that lower the diffusivity of oxidizing or reducing species. This inhibited diffusion limits degradation without compromising the bulk FCC matrix that governs the alloy’s strength and fatigue performance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Si-doped samples should display slower degradation (e.g., lower weight gain/loss, more uniform and adherent surface scales) compared to undoped samples, with the protective effect manifesting as reduced attack along grain boundaries.

hypotheses.boundary: The Si content must remain low (~1 at%) to ensure segregation at grain boundaries rather than formation of secondary silicide phases that might alter the primary FCC matrix properties.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the general concept of grain-boundary passivation by microalloying is supported in other alloy systems (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::010), specific quantitative effects in this FCC high-entropy alloy are not well established.

hypotheses.conditions: Anneal samples in an inert atmosphere to prevent premature oxidation; then expose both annealed and as-built samples to elevated-temperature (≈900 °C for 50–100 hours) oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.

hypotheses.boundary: Annealing must be performed at a temperature low enough to avoid significant grain coarsening or phase transformations (maintaining the FCC structure), yet high enough to relieve residual stresses.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While similar annealing treatments effectively reduce lattice distortions in other systems, the quantitative impact on degradation behavior in this specific FCC high-entropy alloy is not precisely established.

paper_did: Produced an Al0.5CrFeNiTi high entropy alloy from high‐purity elemental powders (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, Ti) using a powder metallurgy route.

Employed mechanical alloying in a planetary ball mill (20 h milling with a 10:1 ball-to‐powder ratio, using N‐heptane as a process control agent) followed by pressing (using 200 kN force with mold release wax) and sintering at various temperatures (750 °C, 875 °C, 1000 °C) under controlled atmospheres.
Characterized the alloyed powders and sintered compacts via SEM, EDS, XRD, particle size distribution, flow rate measurement, density, and porosity evaluations.
paper_reported: Mechanical alloying led to an evolution in the alloying degree with particle agglomeration, shape and size refinement (average particle size ~60.4 µm) and improved homogeneity.
XRD analyses confirmed the formation of FCC, BCC, and HCP phases with peak shifts indicative of refined lattice parameters upon extended milling.

Sintering experiments showed that different thermal treatments affected the microstructure and porosity (with sintering at 875 °C yielding the lowest porosity though larger pores, and sintering at 1000 °C with furnace cooling producing a refined, crack‐free compact).
paper_proposed: Future work aimed at further processing the sintered bulk material to achieve lower porosity and enhanced microstructural integrity.
Exploration of processing parameter optimization to mitigate oxidation and improve the overall performance of the HEA, potentially paving the way for applications in aggressive service environments.

hypotheses.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures (700–1000 °C) in both oxidizing (air or O2-rich) and reducing (e.g. H2-containing) gas environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Reduction of chemical heterogeneity at melt-pool boundaries leading to a more uniform surface chemistry during oxidation.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the as-built state, rapid solidification during AM creates slight microsegregation at interlayer boundaries that serve as preferential sites for oxidation due to local enrichment of more reactive species. This leads to formation of a non-uniform oxide scale that degrades protective performance. Homogenization should disperse these segregated elements, thereby promoting a single, more adherent and protective oxide layer that retards degradation. This builds upon the paper’s findings that oxidation behavior is linked to elemental distribution (see PMC10650386::web::019) and the importance of composition on oxide scale formation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built alloy, the homogenized samples will exhibit a more uniform oxide scale, lower weight gain during oxidation, and reduced oxide spallation. The improvement is expected to be moderate, with a significant change in oxide uniformity.
hypotheses.baseline: As-built AM alloy with inherent microsegregation at layer boundaries and nonuniform oxide formation.
hypotheses.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be operative at temperatures above approximately 700 °C where oxidation kinetics are accelerated; the effect is relevant in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres that actively interact with the reactive segregated phases.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative changes in degradation rate are uncertain due to variable degrees of microsegregation in AM parts.

paper_did: Produced an Al0.5CrFeNiTi high entropy alloy via a powder metallurgy route that involved mechanical alloying (using a planetary ball mill with a 10:1 ball‐to‐powder ratio for up to 20 hours under an Ar atmosphere with 2 wt% N‐heptane as a PCA), cold pressing, and sintering.

Processed and characterized the alloyed powders and consolidated bulk samples by measuring flow properties, free flow and tap densities, and particle size distribution; and by performing SEM, EDS, and XRD analyses to monitor microstructural evolution and phase formation.
Performed theoretical calculations (enthalpy of mixing, entropy of mixing, atomic size difference, solid solution formation parameter, and valence electron concentration) to predict phase formation.
paper_reported: The alloy exhibited successful mixing and refinement of particle size with increased milling time, achieving an average particle size of ~60.4 µm and improved homogeneity.

XRD analyses confirmed the presence of FCC, BCC, and HCP phases—with key peaks (e.g. at 44.6° and 43.5°) reflecting the contribution of all constituent elements—and indicated lattice refinement after extended milling.

Sintering experiments at different temperatures (750 °C, 875 °C, and 1000 °C with varied cooling regimes) showed that higher sintering temperatures improved consolidation (reducing pore sizes) though overall porosity remained in the 21–23% range, and minor oxidation was observed.
paper_proposed: Future processing efforts to further reduce the porosity of the bulk material, enhancing its structural integrity and mechanical performance.
